etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English free, fre, freo, from Old English frēo (“free”), from Proto-West Germanic *frī, from Proto-Germanic *frijaz (“beloved, not in bondage”), from Proto-Indo-European *priHós (“pleased, loved”), from *preyH- (“to please, love”). Related to friend.

definitions.definition: Not imprisoned or enslaved.
Generous; liberal.
(obsolete) Clear of offence or crime; guiltless; innocent.

quote.citation: 1679, John Dryden, Oedipus: A Tragedy, page 59:
quote.text: My hands are guilty, but my heart is free.

definitions.definition: Without obligations.
To be enjoyed by anyone freely.

quote.citation: 1590-2, William Shakespeare, Taming of the Shrew, I, ii:
quote.text: Why, sir, I pray, are not the streets as free / For me as for you?

definitions.definition: (of a government, country) Upholding individual rights.
(software) With no or only freedom-preserving limitations on distribution or modification.
(software) Intended for release, as opposed to a checked version.
(social) Unconstrained.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Quickly, spirit! / Thou shalt ere long be free.

quote.citation: 1899, Stephen Crane, chapter 1, in Twelve O'Clock:
quote.text: There was some laughter, and Roddle was left free to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town. “Mason Rickets, he had ten big punkins a-sittin' in front of his store, an' them fellers from the Upside-down-F ranch shot 'em up  […] .”

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, Schumpeter, “Cronies and capitols”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: Policing the relationship between government and business in a free society is difficult. Businesspeople have every right to lobby governments, and civil servants to take jobs in the private sector.

definitions.definition: (by extension, chiefly used in advertising) Complimentary.
Obtainable without any payment.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “The attack of the MOOCs”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Since the launch early last year of […] two Silicon Valley start-ups offering free education through MOOCs, massive open online courses, the ivory towers of academia have been shaken to their foundations. University brands built in some cases over centuries have been forced to contemplate the possibility that information technology will rapidly make their existing business model obsolete.

definitions.definition: (group theory, of a group) Having a set of generators which satisfy no non-trivial relations; equivalently, being the group of reduced words on a set of generators.
(commutative algebra, of a module) Having a linearly independent set of generators (called a basis).
(algebra, of an algebraic structure) In any of various technical senses generic, universal.
(logic, of a variable) Unconstrained by quantifiers.
(programming) Unconstrained of identifiers, not bound.
(linguistics) (of a morpheme) That can be used by itself, unattached to another morpheme.
(abstract) Unconstrained.
Unobstructed, without blockages.
Unattached or uncombined.
Not currently in use; not taken; unoccupied.
(botany, mycology) Not attached; loose.

quote.citation: 1992, Rudolf M[athias] Schuster, The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America: East of the Hundredth Meridian, volume V, Chicago, Ill.: Field Museum of Natural History, →ISBN, page 7:
quote.text: Furthermore, the free anterior margin of the lobule is arched toward the lobe and is often involute […]

definitions.definition: (military) Of a rocket or missile: not under the control of a guidance system after being launched.
(physical) Unconstrained.
Without; not containing (what is specified); exempt; clear; liberated.

quote.citation: 1679-1715, Gilbert Burnet, The History of the Reformation of the Church of England:
quote.text: princes declaring themselves free from the obligations of their treaties

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: One morning I had been driven to the precarious refuge afforded by the steps of the inn, after rejecting offers from the Celebrity to join him in a variety of amusements. But even here I was not free from interruption, for he was seated on a horse-block below me, playing with a fox terrier.

definitions.definition: (dated) Ready; eager; acting without spurring or whipping; spirited.
(dated) Invested with a particular freedom or franchise; enjoying certain immunities or privileges; admitted to special rights; followed by of.

quote.citation: 1697, John Dryden, “Part 3, line 1245”, in The Hind and the Panther:
quote.text: He therefore makes all birds, of every sect, / Free of his farm.

definitions.definition: (UK, law, obsolete) Certain or honourable; the opposite of base.
(law) Privileged or individual; proprietary.
Without needing to pay.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “The Glasgow Suburban Electrification is opened”, in Trains Illustrated, page 714:
quote.text: Above all, the 48-page timetables of the new service, which have been distributed free at every station in the scheme, are a model to the rest of B.R. For the first time on British Railways, so far as we are aware, a substantial timetable has been produced, not only without a single footnote but also devoid of all wearisome asterisks, stars, letter suffixes and other hieroglyphics.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Freely; willingly.

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602, William Shakespeare, Henry VIII, published 1623:
quote.text: I as free forgive you / As I would be forgiven.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make free; set at liberty; release.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], page 5:
quote.text: Pro. […] Spirit, fine ſpirit, Ile free thee / Within two dayes for this.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To rid of something that confines or oppresses. [with from]

quote.citation: 1885, Richard F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Night 564:
quote.text: Then I walked about, till I found on the further side, a great river of sweet water, running with a strong current; whereupon I called to mind the boat-raft I had made aforetime and said to myself, "Needs must I make another; haply I may free me from this strait. If I escape, I have my desire and I vow to Allah Almighty to forswear travel; and if I perish I shall be at peace and shall rest from toil and moil."

definitions.definition: (transitive, programming) To relinquish (previously allocated memory) to the system.

quote.citation: 2002, Jesse Liberty, SAMS Teach Yourself C++ in 24 Hours, page 148:
quote.text: There is no way to access that original area of memory, nor is there any way to free it before the program ends.

definitions.definition: (Australian rules football, Gaelic football) Abbreviation of free kick.

quote.text: Whether deserved or not, the free gave Cresswell the chance to cover himself in glory with a shot on goal after the siren.

definitions.definition: (soccer) A free transfer.

quote.citation: 2011 September 21, Sam Lyon, “Man City 2 - 0 Birmingham”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: Hargreaves, who left Manchester United on a free during the summer, drilled a 22-yard beauty to open the scoring.

definitions.definition: (hurling) The usual means of restarting play after a foul is committed, where the non-offending team restarts from where the foul was committed.
(swimming, informal) Abbreviation of freestyle.
